title: Take the contradiction seriously instead of dismissing it
explanation: `df -h /var/spool/ingest` shows free space, yet writes still fail with `No space left on device`. That's not a fluke — a filesystem tracks two separate, independently exhaustible resources: data blocks (bytes) and inodes (the fixed-size table of metadata entries, one required per file regardless of that file's size). `df -h` only reports the first one.

title: Check the resource df -h doesn't show
explanation: `df -i /var/spool/ingest` reports IUse% — inode utilization — separately from byte usage. Seeing it at 100% confirms the real constraint: every inode this filesystem was provisioned with (`nr_inodes=200` on this tmpfs) is already consumed, so `open(..., O_CREAT)` fails at the metadata layer even though plenty of bytes are still free.

title: Find what consumed them
explanation: `ls -1 /var/spool/ingest | wc -l` shows a huge count of tiny leftover `.tmp` files — each one, no matter how small, costs exactly one inode. A worker that creates temp files and never cleans them up can exhaust an inode table long before it comes anywhere close to filling the filesystem's actual byte capacity.

title: Delete with find, not a shell glob
explanation: `rm /var/spool/ingest/*.tmp` can fail outright with *Argument list too long* once the file count is this high, because the shell has to expand the glob into a single command line before `rm` ever runs. `sudo find /var/spool/ingest -name '*.tmp' -delete` walks and removes files one at a time without ever building that giant argument list.

title: Verify with the same command that caught the real cause
explanation: Re-running `df -i /var/spool/ingest` (not `df -h`) confirms inodes are actually free again, and successfully creating a new file proves the fix worked at the layer that was actually broken.
